sections.h2: What does a house sale in Lakewood, NJ involve?
sections.html:
Lakewood is a flat, fast-growing township in Ocean County, and a house here moves through township code enforcement, an Ocean County recording office and a state fee schedule before the deed changes hands. Whether an agent lists it, you sell it yourself or a buyer pays cash for it as-is, each route ends at the same three desks.

Lakewood has more residents than any other township in Ocean County, spread across 24.68 square miles of land. The 2025 Census estimate is 143,765 residents, up from 135,158 in the 2020 count. Households here average 4.36 people, so floor plan and bedroom count weigh heavily when a buyer looks at a house.

sections.h2: Where did Lakewood come from, and what is the terrain?
sections.html:
Lakewood began as a sawmill and bog-iron area in the 1700s. It was called Bricksburg in 1865, renamed Lakewood in 1880 as a winter resort, and chartered as a township by the state legislature on March 23, 1892, with land from Brick. Cranberry bogs and pine woods made way for large developments in the 1960s, and Leisure Village went on sale in 1963.

Lakewood lies on the flat coastal plain, with about three quarters of the land between 20 and 80 feet above sea level. The Metedeconk River's North Branch marks the northern line and part of the eastern line, and four man-made lakes (Carasaljo, Manetta, Shenandoah and Waddill) anchor several neighborhoods. Greenville, Seven Stars, South Lakewood and Lake Carasaljo are place names you will see on listings. The township touches Brick, Jackson, Toms River and Howell.

The Census counts the Lakewood area as a CDP of 69,398 people in 2020, with the age-restricted Leisure Village and Leisure Village East communities counted separately at 4,966 and 4,189. If your house is in one of those communities, request its own resale rules in writing before you sign a contract.

sections.h2: How big are Lakewood households and home values?
sections.html:
The Census counts 4.36 people in the average Lakewood household. Just over half of homes (51.5%) have their owner living in them, and the middle owner-occupied home is valued at $466,700.

A median household income near $65,000 beside a $466,700 median home value means many buyers lean on mortgages, family money or cash. That is one reason as-is offers are common on tired or oddly laid-out houses here.

Education and health care lead. For 2022 the Census lists about $1.54 billion in health care and social assistance revenue and about $3.25 billion in retail sales. Beth Medrash Govoha, founded in 1943, is the largest yeshiva outside Israel, and Georgian Court University has sat on Lake Carasaljo since 1924.

Part of the township was a state Urban Enterprise Zone from 1994, and that status expired in October 2025. The zone helped fund ShoreTown Ballpark, the 6,588-seat home of the Jersey Shore BlueClaws. If a buyer asks about sales-tax treatment of nearby stores, point them to the township instead of guessing.

sections.h2: What schools and commuting routes affect resale value?
sections.html:
The Lakewood School District runs eight schools with 5,433 students in the 2021-22 school year, and the district also buses students to private schools, which reached about 25,000 students at yeshivas and other schools by 2016. Many families choose a home by walking distance to a yeshiva or school rather than by the public school zone, so ask your agent which side of a street a buyer would prefer.

Buyers usually ask about these links:

  • Garden State Parkway exit 89, which also feeds Route 70 after exit 88 closed permanently in November 2014.
  • Route 70, Route 88 and Route 9, plus county roads 526, 528, 547 and 549.
  • The Lakewood Bus Terminal, where NJ Transit routes 137 and 139 run toward New York's Port Authority, 317 toward Philadelphia, 67 toward Newark and 559 toward Atlantic City.
  • The in-town Lakewood Shuttle and Ocean Ride routes OC3 and OC4.

sections.h2: What does Lakewood's code enforcement office require before a sale?
sections.html:
Start with the Township of Lakewood's Code Enforcement office at 212 4th Street, phone 732-364-3760. Its rental and housing window runs 8:30 AM to 4 PM, and its page carries a legal notice to residential property owners about smoke alarms and carbon monoxide alarms. Ask the staff what resale paperwork and inspection your closing date needs, and request the form list in writing.

One question in the township's FAQ asks whether a certificate of occupancy is required when selling a home, so get the current answer by phone. Ask about open permits too. The office warns that the penalty for unpermitted work can reach $2,000, with another $2,000 added for every week the violation continues.

  • Permit review under the state construction code can take up to 20 business days.
  • The engineering section of the township FAQ covers flood zone lookups and elevation certificates, property surveys and wetlands questions.
  • A rented house also needs a rental certificate of occupancy application on file ahead of a tenant change.

sections.h2: Who records a Lakewood deed, and what does the seller owe?
sections.html:
Lakewood deeds are recorded by the Ocean County Clerk, whose main office (118 Washington Street, Toms River) answers at (732) 929-2018. Posted hours are weekdays 8 to 4:30, with counter service ending at 4. The clerk's contact page also lists a Lakewood location at 225 4th Street, Room 211, phone (732) 370-8850.

Since Lakewood's median home value is $466,700, a typical sale falls under the state schedule for prices above $350,000. The seller owes that fee, and the rate climbs in steps as the price rises. Sales above $1 million add a graduated percentage fee of 1% to 3.5%, also charged to the seller.

For back taxes, request a payoff figure from the township's tax collector. The township advertised an online sale of 2025 and prior-year delinquent taxes and water or sewer charges with a sale date of October 28, 2026, so accounts that were not redeemed may carry a certificate now.

sections.h2: Which sale route suits a Lakewood house?
sections.html:
Choose by timeline and condition. A listing reaches the widest set of buyers, but it comes with showings, an appraisal and a township inspection step. Selling alone saves the commission and leaves the paperwork with you. A buyer paying cash for the house as-is removes repairs and loan approval from the picture; compare written terms, including who pays the transfer fee and who orders any township certificate.

Pull together the survey, permit records, current leases and the latest tax bill before anyone makes an offer. Clean paperwork keeps Lakewood deals moving, while a late permit or occupancy question tends to stall them.

faqs.q: Is a township inspection part of selling in Lakewood?
faqs.a: Ask the township. Code Enforcement at 732-364-3760 handles smoke and carbon monoxide alarm rules and resale paperwork, and its FAQ lists a certificate of occupancy question for home sellers. Get the requirement for your address from them before fixing a closing date.

faqs.q: Is the transfer fee my cost as a Lakewood seller?
faqs.a: Yes. The state bases it on the price in the deed and collects it when the Ocean County Clerk records the deed. Sales above $1 million also trigger a graduated percentage fee, again on the seller.

faqs.q: Which office records a Lakewood deed?
faqs.a: The Ocean County Clerk. The main office is in Toms River at (732) 929-2018, and the clerk's contact page lists a Lakewood location at 225 4th Street, Room 211, (732) 370-8850.

faqs.q: What if my Lakewood house has open permits?
faqs.a: You can still sell, but deal with them first. Code Enforcement can tell you which permits are open, and unpermitted work can draw fines that grow weekly. A buyer or lender may require the permit closed before the sale.

faqs.q: Is cash faster than listing in Lakewood?
faqs.a: Often, because a cash sale skips mortgage approval and an appraisal. A listing may reach more buyers. Deed recording, the transfer fee and any township certificate apply either way, so compare the written terms.
